lessons.title: An Inspector Calls: characters
lessons.summary: Get to know the Birlings, Gerald, the Inspector and the unseen Eva Smith, and learn how Priestley builds each character to carry part of his argument about responsibility.
objectives: I can describe the personality, role and function of each main character.
I can explain how Priestley uses stage directions and speech to shape our view of characters.
I can track how Sheila and Eric change across the play, and why the older characters do not.
I can explain the symbolic roles of the Inspector and Eva Smith.
I can write analytically about a character using precise evidence.

activities.title: Inspector Goole: the voice of conscience
activities.content:
## Inspector Goole

The Inspector is the engine of the play. He arrives uninvited, takes control of the room and does not leave until every character has confessed. Priestley's stage directions describe him as a man of **massiveness, solidity and purposefulness**, and he stays calm while the family grows more agitated. Notice that he is not physically large: his power comes from certainty.

**His method.** He questions one person at a time, refuses to show the photograph to more than one person, and cuts through excuses with blunt statements about the girl's death. He does not accuse; he lets the characters condemn themselves.

**His name.** *Goole* sounds like *ghoul*, a spirit linked with death, and *Inspector* suggests someone who looks closely. After the twist, we never learn who or what he was. Possible readings: a ghost, a figure of conscience, a time-traveller from the future, or simply Priestley's own voice. What matters in an essay is what he **does**: he forces the truth into the open.

**His message.** His final speech insists that we are all responsible for one another and warns of fire and blood if the lesson is ignored. Written in 1945, this echoes the two world wars the audience had just lived through. He is a **mouthpiece** for Priestley's socialist beliefs, and a **dramatic device** for making those beliefs tense and theatrical rather than preachy.

activities.title: Reading a character through stage directions
activities.content:
Stage directions are Priestley's most direct way of telling us who a character is. Always treat them as evidence.

| Stage direction (paraphrased) | What it tells us | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| The Inspector is to give an impression of massiveness, solidity and purposefulness | He has moral weight; he cannot be moved | "Priestley's demand for *solidity* makes the Inspector a fixed point against which the family's excuses break." |
| The lighting should change from pink and intimate to brighter and harder when he arrives | The comfortable illusion is switched off; nothing can be hidden | "The shift from soft pink light to a harder glare turns the dining room into an interrogation room." |
| The Inspector looks hard at each person before speaking | He weighs people; he already seems to know | "His habit of staring before he speaks suggests he is not gathering evidence but confronting them with what he knows." |

**Rule of thumb:** quote the key word from the stage direction, then explain what it makes the audience feel or expect.

question.text: Which statement best describes the Inspector's method of questioning?
question.hint: Think about the photograph, the order of confessions, and who does most of the talking.
question.explanation: The Inspector deals with one person at a time, shows the photograph to only one character at once, and lets each of them reveal their own guilt. This builds the chain of events and keeps control in his hands.

options.text: He questions one character at a time and lets each of them expose their own guilt
He shows everyone the photograph together so they can compare stories
options.feedback: He deliberately shows it to only one person at a time, which later lets Gerald suggest it was a trick.

options.text: He shouts accusations and threatens the family with arrest
options.feedback: He stays calm and never threatens legal action; his power is moral.

options.text: He asks Birling to explain everything on behalf of the family

activities.title: Arthur and Sybil Birling: the older generation
activities.content:
## Arthur Birling

Birling is a self-made factory owner, a former Lord Mayor, and a man who cares intensely about status. He hopes for a knighthood and keeps mentioning it. Priestley describes him as **hard-headed** and provincial in speech, hinting that despite his money he is not quite a gentleman, which is why he is so eager to please Gerald's aristocratic parents.

His long speeches in Act One are packed with **dramatic irony**: he insists war is impossible and that a famous new liner cannot sink. The 1945 audience knew better, so before the Inspector even arrives, Birling's judgement has been destroyed. His belief that each man should look after himself is the exact opposite of the Inspector's message.

Under questioning he is defensive and blustering. He sacked Eva to keep wages low, and he cannot see any link between that and her death. At the end he cares only about avoiding a public scandal.

## Sybil Birling

Mrs Birling is her husband's social superior and described as a **rather cold woman**. She polices manners, corrects her family, and treats the working class as a different species. Her prejudice against Eva as a girl of *that class* leads her to refuse charity help.

She is the only character who never admits any fault. Her condemnation of the unknown father, which turns out to be Eric, exposes her **hypocrisy** and makes her the sharpest example of the older generation's refusal to learn.

question.text: Match each detail to what it reveals about Mr or Mrs Birling.
question.hint: Think about status, prejudice, dramatic irony and refusal to accept blame.
question.explanation: Birling's talk of a knighthood shows his obsession with status. His confident prediction about the liner is dramatic irony. Mrs Birling's dismissal of Eva as a girl of that class shows class prejudice. Her insistence she did nothing wrong shows she refuses responsibility.

pairs.left: Birling keeps mentioning a possible knighthood
pairs.right: He is obsessed with social status and climbing higher

pairs.left: Birling declares the new liner cannot sink
pairs.right: Dramatic irony undermines his judgement for the audience

pairs.left: Mrs Birling dismisses Eva as a girl of that class
pairs.right: Class prejudice shapes her treatment of others

pairs.left: Mrs Birling insists she did nothing she is ashamed of
pairs.right: She refuses to accept any responsibility

activities.title: Sheila and Eric: the younger generation
activities.content:
## Sheila Birling

Sheila begins as a pleased, slightly spoilt young woman celebrating her engagement, described in the stage directions as **very pleased with life**. Her change is the clearest in the play.

When she learns she had Eva sacked from Milwards, she is horrified and does not try to excuse herself. From that point she becomes the Inspector's ally. She warns her mother not to build a wall between herself and the girl, she sees where the questioning is heading before anyone else, and she is the first to say that whether the Inspector was real makes no difference. By the end she speaks with a maturity that her parents lack, and she refuses to take Gerald's ring back until she has thought properly.

## Eric Birling

Eric is introduced as **half shy, half assertive**, and his drinking is hinted at from the first scene. He is uneasy with his father's views and is squashed whenever he tries to speak. His part in Eva's story is the most serious: he forced himself on her while drunk, made her pregnant, and stole from his father to support her.

Yet Eric, like Sheila, accepts his guilt. His anger at his mother for turning Eva away is one of the play's most powerful moments. He also attacks his father for caring only about scandal. Through Eric, Priestley shows both the damage a privileged, neglected young man can do and the possibility of change.

activities.title: Tracking Sheila's development
activities.content:
Examiners love a character who **changes**, because you can structure an answer around the change. Here is Sheila across the three acts.

| Point in play | Evidence (paraphrased) | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Act One, opening | Excited about the ring; teases Gerald about last summer | Playful, a little naive, but already suspicious |
| Act One, confession | Admits she complained about Eva out of jealousy and says she would never do it again | Immediate guilt; capacity to change |
| Act Two | Tells her mother not to build a wall; says the Inspector is breaking down their defences | Insight; she understands the Inspector's method |
| Act Three | Insists the family did those things whether the Inspector was real or not | Moral clarity; she has become the Inspector's voice after he leaves |

**Model sentence:** Priestley moves Sheila from the girlish delight of the opening to the moral clarity of Act Three, so that by the end she, not the Inspector, is the voice challenging her parents.

Try building the same table for **Eric** or, as a contrast, for **Birling**, who barely moves at all.

question.text: Complete the sentences about Sheila and Eric.

metadata.blanksText: Sheila had Eva dismissed from ___ after a fit of jealousy. Eric stole money from his father's ___ to support Eva. Both are examples of the ___ generation, who accept responsibility and change.

question.hint: The department store; the place Birling keeps his business; the opposite of older.
question.explanation: Sheila's complaint got Eva sacked from Milwards. Eric took money from his father's office (the firm). Priestley uses Sheila and Eric to represent the younger generation, who are capable of learning.

activities.title: Gerald, Eva Smith and Edna
activities.content:
## Gerald Croft

Gerald is the son of a titled family and a rising businessman. He agrees with Birling's views and is comfortable in the world of money and influence. Priestley places him **between the generations**: he is young enough to change, but chooses not to.

His story with Daisy Renton is more complicated than the others. He rescued her from a predatory man, gave her shelter and, as Sheila admits, was probably the only person who was kind to her. But he also used her as a mistress and ended it when it suited him. He shows genuine sorrow when he learns she is dead. Yet in Act Three it is Gerald who works out that the Inspector might be a fake, and he immediately tries to return to normal, offering Sheila the ring as if nothing has happened. His charm hides a refusal to learn.

## Eva Smith

Eva never appears on stage, yet she is the centre of the play. Everything we know comes from the Inspector and the family. Her ordinary name suggests she stands for all working-class women; the Inspector says there are millions like her. She is a **symbol** of the powerless, and her absence means the audience must imagine her, which makes her more powerful than any actor could be.

## Edna

The maid has only a few lines, but she is the only working-class person we see. She opens the door to the Inspector and is ordered about without thanks, a quiet reminder of the class the Birlings depend on and ignore.

question.text: True or false: by the end of the play Gerald, like Sheila and Eric, fully accepts responsibility for what happened to Eva Smith.
question.hint: Think about what Gerald does after he returns from talking to the policeman in Act Three.
question.explanation: False. Although Gerald shows real sadness when he learns of Daisy's death, in Act Three he leads the effort to prove the Inspector was a hoax and then offers Sheila the ring again, wanting to return to normal. He sides with the older generation.

options.text: True
False

question.text: Explain why Priestley chose never to show Eva Smith on stage, and how this affects the audience.
question.hint: Think about her name, the idea that there are millions like her, and what an audience does when it cannot see a character.
question.explanation: Keeping Eva off stage lets her represent all exploited working-class women rather than one individual; the Inspector says there are millions of Eva Smiths. The audience must imagine her from the family's accounts, which makes them active participants and prevents the character being reduced to one actor. Her absence also mirrors her powerlessness: she has no voice in a world run by people like the Birlings.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that her absence allows her to represent or symbolise many working-class people
Explains that the audience must imagine her, making her more powerful or the audience more involved
Links her absence to her lack of voice or power in society

question.text:
How does Priestley present the difference between the older and younger generations in An Inspector Calls? Write about:

- how the older and younger characters respond to the Inspector
- how Priestley uses these differences to convey his ideas.
question.hint: Contrast Birling and Mrs Birling with Sheila and Eric. Consider Gerald's position, the reactions to the hoax, and what Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to feel about the future.
question.explanation: A strong answer contrasts the older generation's denial (Birling's concern with scandal, Mrs Birling's refusal to accept blame) with the younger generation's guilt and growth (Sheila's insight, Eric's anger and remorse). It places Gerald with the older generation despite his age, uses the hoax reaction as the clearest test, and explains that Priestley presents the young as the hope for a fairer post-war society, using the Inspector's line that the young are more impressionable.

markScheme.criterion: Describes the older generation's refusal to accept responsibility, with a specific example (Birling's fear of scandal, Mrs Birling's denial)
Describes Sheila's change or growing insight with a specific example
Describes Eric's guilt or his confrontation with his parents
Places Gerald with the older generation or explains his refusal to change
Uses the reaction to the hoax or the ending as evidence of who has learnt the lesson
Explains Priestley's purpose: the young as hope for a fairer or more responsible future society

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Inspector Goole**: calm, solid, purposeful; questions one at a time; a mouthpiece for Priestley's belief in collective responsibility; his true nature is left open.
- **Arthur Birling**: self-made, status-hungry capitalist; undermined by dramatic irony; never accepts blame.
- **Sybil Birling**: cold, class-prejudiced, hypocritical; condemns the father who turns out to be her son; admits nothing.
- **Sheila**: changes most; becomes the Inspector's ally and voice.
- **Eric**: troubled, drinking, guilty of the worst act, but accepts responsibility and turns on his parents.
- **Gerald**: charming, kind to Eva for a while, but chooses the older generation's comfort over change.
- **Eva Smith**: never seen; a symbol of the powerless; **Edna** is the only working-class person on stage.
- Use **stage directions** as evidence and structure answers around **change** and **contrast**.

practiceQuestions.text: Which character is described in the stage directions as a rather cold woman who is her husband's social superior?
practiceQuestions.hint: She chairs a charity committee and is proud of her position.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sybil Birling is described as cold and socially superior to her husband, which explains both her snobbery and her prejudice against Eva.

options.text: Sybil Birling
Sheila Birling
Eva Smith
Edna

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Eva Smith appears on stage in Act Three to confront the Birlings.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how the audience learns about Eva.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Eva never appears on stage. Everything we know about her comes from the Inspector and the family's confessions, which makes her a symbol rather than an individual.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: What does the Inspector's surname, Goole, most likely suggest?
practiceQuestions.hint: Say it aloud and think of a word linked to death and spirits.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Goole sounds like ghoul, a ghostly figure linked with death. It hints that the Inspector may be supernatural, or at least not an ordinary policeman.

options.text: It sounds like 'ghoul', hinting that he may be a ghostly or supernatural figure
It is the name of the town where the Birlings live
It shows he is a wealthy aristocrat
It is a common surname for policemen in 1912

practiceQuestions.text: Match each character to a description of their role in the play.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about who changes, who refuses to, and who stands for a whole class.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Inspector is Priestley's mouthpiece. Sheila changes the most. Birling is the voice of self-interested capitalism. Eva is the absent symbol of the exploited working class.

pairs.right: A dramatic device and mouthpiece for Priestley's message
The character who changes most and adopts the Inspector's views
The voice of self-interested capitalism, undermined by dramatic irony
An unseen symbol of the exploited working class

metadata.blanksText: Gerald met Eva, who was then calling herself Daisy ___, in the Palace bar and later set her up in a friend's ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Her second surname; the place she lived while she was his mistress.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eva used the name Daisy Renton when Gerald met her, and he installed her in a friend's flat (rooms) for the summer.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following show that Eric accepts responsibility for his actions?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what Eric says and does in Act Three after the Inspector leaves.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eric admits what he did and angrily blames his mother for refusing Eva help, and he sides with Sheila in insisting their actions were real whether or not the Inspector was. Stealing money and drinking are part of his guilt, not signs of accepting it.

options.text: He confronts his mother for turning Eva away from the charity
He agrees with Sheila that it makes no difference whether the Inspector was real
He steals money from his father's office
options.feedback: This is part of what he did wrong, not a sign of accepting responsibility.

options.text: He drinks heavily during the celebration dinner

practiceQuestions.text: Put the characters in the order in which the Inspector questions them.
practiceQuestions.hint: Father first, then daughter, then the fiancé, then the mother, then the son.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birling is questioned first, then Sheila, then Gerald, then Mrs Birling, and finally Eric, matching the order of events in Eva's life.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how Priestley uses dramatic irony to shape the audience's view of Arthur Birling in Act One.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about his predictions about war and the new liner, and what the 1945 audience knew.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birling confidently predicts lasting peace and praises the new liner as unsinkable. The 1945 audience knew that the ship sank and that two world wars followed, so his confidence makes him look foolish. This dramatic irony discredits him and his self-interested views before the Inspector even arrives, so the audience is prepared to side with the Inspector.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies a specific mistaken prediction (no war, the unsinkable liner, lasting prosperity)
Explains that the audience knows these predictions are wrong because of when the play was written or performed
Explains the effect: Birling and his views are discredited or seem foolish, so the audience sides against him

practiceQuestions.text: Why might Priestley have made Gerald partly sympathetic in his treatment of Eva?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how a purely villainous Gerald would change the play's message.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gerald's kindness to Daisy makes the point that even well-meaning people can exploit the vulnerable when they hold power. If all the characters were simply cruel, the audience could distance themselves; Gerald's mixture forces them to examine their own behaviour.

options.text: To show that even kind, well-meaning people can exploit the vulnerable, so the audience cannot dismiss the message as being about villains
To suggest that Eva's death was entirely her own fault
Because Gerald is based on Priestley himself
To make the audience side with Birling's views about business

practiceQuestions.text: How does Priestley present Sheila as a character who changes during the play? Refer to at least two different points in the play.
practiceQuestions.hint: Contrast her excitement in the opening with her confession, her warnings to her mother in Act Two, and her refusal to pretend nothing happened in Act Three.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A good answer contrasts the playful, pleased Sheila of the opening with her immediate guilt after the Milwards confession; notes her growing insight in Act Two as she warns her mother and recognises the Inspector's method; shows her moral authority in Act Three when she insists the events were real; and explains that Priestley uses her change to model the response he wants from the audience and to represent hope in the younger generation.

markScheme.criterion: Describes Sheila's initial character (pleased, excited, playful, naive) with reference to the opening
Refers to her confession about Milwards and her immediate acceptance of guilt
Refers to her insight in Act Two (warning her mother, understanding the Inspector's method)
Refers to her stance in Act Three that the events were real whether or not the Inspector was
Explains Priestley's purpose in presenting her change (model for the audience, hope in the young)
